titleStmt.title: Letter from John Chamberlain to Dudley Carleton, 15 February 1599

publicationStmt.p: Published digitally at earlymodernletters.org. Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

div.p: Because yt is long since I heard from you, I did verely thincke when I saw Sir Gerrat Harvy in PowlesSt. Paul's Cathedral and its surrounding nave walk served as the great indoor exchange of Elizabethan London — the place where merchants, lawyers, soldiers, and gentlemen loitered and passed news. Chamberlain ran into Harvey there and tried to extract intelligence about Carleton's situation at Ostend. that your Lord had ben arrived, but understanding by him that your conge was not come from the HagheCarleton, serving under the Lord Governor of Ostend, required formal leave from the English representative at The Hague before he could return to England. Harvey, who had just come from the Netherlands, confirmed that this leave had not yet been granted. at his departure, I made account we may looke after you a moneth more at the least, yf not longer. I am going to Knebworth (I know not how soone) and mean to tarry there all Lent. Yf you come over in this interim let us intreat your companie, yf yt may be spared.

Our provisions for Ireland go forward with leaden feet, and the erle of Essex his commission is no neerer signing (in shew) then when I wrote last; the jarres continue as they did, yf not worse, by dayly renewing, and our musicke runs so much upon discords, that I feare what harmonie they will make of yt in the end. Many thinges passe which may not be written, but in conclusion, Iliacos intra muros peccatur et extra:"There is sin within the walls of Troy as well as without" — Horace, Epistles 1.2.16. Chamberlain applies the line to the Essex-Cecil-Queen quarrel: blame cannot be assigned to one party only. The quotation would have been instantly recognisable to Carleton. there is fault on all sides, and quicquid delirant reges plectuntur Achivi, "Whatever madness kings indulge in, the Greeks are punished" — Horace, Epistles 1.2.14. The Achivi (Greeks) are ordinary subjects: Chamberlain and Carleton's circle pay the price for quarrels among the great. The two Horatian quotations together frame the Essex affair as a classical tragedy-in-progress. whosoever offends the common wealth is punished.

Here is a benevolenceA "benevolence" was a forced "voluntary" contribution levied by the crown without parliamentary consent — notionally a gift, in practice a tax. The breadth of the demand here — spanning every branch of the common law and equity courts, the chancery, the duchy, and even the civilians at the Arches — was unusually sweeping and reflects how acute the crown's financial need had become. demaunded of all manner of the lawyers, not only of the Innes of Court, but officers and clarks of the exchecquer, kinges bench, common pleas, court of wardes, star chamber, chauncery, Duchy of Lancaster, auditors, recevers and the rest, not forgetting the poore Doctors of the Arches;The Doctors of the Arches were the civilian (canon and civil law) lawyers who practised in the Court of Arches, the principal ecclesiastical appeal court for the province of Canterbury, held at Doctors' Commons near St. Paul's. Chamberlain's "poore" is gently ironic: they were not notably poor, but they were the most marginal of the legal professions being tapped, and their inclusion signals the crown scraping the bottom of the barrel. there was some curtesie made at the first, but in the end they must geve downe theyre milke, and whether from them yt shall proceed over all England yt is doubtfull.

Two dayes since we had a proclamation that no Englishman going to sea upon paine of death take any that were in amitie with her Majestie, either Italians, French, Lowe Countrie men, Danes, or of the Haunse townes, but only meere Spaniards or subjects to the king of Spaine.A tightening of the prize-taking order first mentioned in Letter 16, now extended beyond the Levant to any sea and to all of England's allied or neutral trading partners. The Dutch, Danes, and Hanseatic merchants were the backbone of the northern European carrying trade; English privateers taking their ships had caused repeated diplomatic protests. The penalty of death signals the crown's determination to enforce the order, but Chamberlain's flat reportage suggests he is not entirely convinced it will hold. I heare that the erle of Essex is much offended with Sir Fra: VereSir Francis Vere (1560–1609), commander of the English forces in the Dutch States' service; Governor of the Brill. Essex had been sending captains to the Low Countries to swell the contingent available for transfer to Ireland; Vere refused to receive them, on the grounds that they were not chosen through the proper channel of the States-General. The resulting clash pitted Essex's authority as incoming Lord Lieutenant of Ireland against Vere's established command in the Netherlands. for refusing the captaines that were lately sent over into the Low Countries.

The Quene removed to Richmont on Satterday last, and on Monday we had a great marriage in towne of younge TerringamIdentified as a member of the Tyringham family of Tyringham, Buckinghamshire; the exact given name is not recorded in the sources available. with a daughter of Sir Thomas GorgeSir Thomas Gorge (1536–1610), courtier and groom of the privy chamber. He married Helena Snakenborg (see Lady Marchioness, below), and their daughter is the bride here. by the Lady Marquesse,Helena Gorge (née Snakenborg, c. 1549–1635), a Swedish noblewoman who came to England in 1565 in the train of Princess Cecilia of Sweden. After the death of William Parr, Marquess of Northampton, whose household she had joined, she married Sir Thomas Gorge in 1576 and continued to be known as "the Lady Marchioness" from her connection to the Parr family title. She was one of the most distinctive figures at the Elizabethan court. and the next weeke we shall have an other of younge DunsWilliam Dunche (later knighted 1603), son of Edmund Dunche of Wittenham, Berkshire. with a daughter of Sir Henry Cromwells.Sir Henry Cromwell (c. 1537–1603) of Hinchinbrook, Huntingdonshire, known as "the Golden Knight" for his celebrated hospitality. His granddaughter would marry Robert Hampden; his grandson Oliver, born in 1599, would become Lord Protector of the Commonwealth — though that was still far in the future from where Chamberlain stood. I heare the match is concluded for younge VaneFrancis Fane (c. 1583–1629), later created first Earl of Westmorland (1624). Chamberlain writes "Vane," a period spelling of Fane; the two names were confused in Elizabethan usage. He was the son of Sir Francis Fane and Mary Neville, through whom his claim to be "Lord of Abergevennie" descended — the Neville barony of Abergavenny having passed through the female line. (that standes to be Lord of Abergevennie) with the daughter of Sir Antony Mildmay.Sir Anthony Mildmay (c. 1550–1617), of Apethorpe, Northamptonshire; diplomat and courtier, son of Sir Walter Mildmay, the Elizabethan statesman and founder of Emmanuel College, Cambridge. His daughter Mary Mildmay became Fane's wife.
Thus you see for want of better marchandise this pettie ware must serve the turne. And so I bid you farewell with my best wishes and commendations.

postscript.p: To my very goode frend Master Dudley Carleton attending on the Lord Governor of Ostend geve these.
